items.definition: Damage or disruption caused by people inside an organisation — either on purpose (a disgruntled worker) or by mistake. Includes theft or loss of physical equipment, data or software/licences, and the use of unauthorised software.
items.examples: An employee copying the customer database to a USB stick before resigning; a worker installing pirated software that brings malware onto the network.
items.examTip: Internal threats come from people with legitimate access, so they are harder to detect than external ones. Always say WHO and WHAT they did.
keyFacts: Can be deliberate (revenge, theft) or accidental (carelessness)
Theft/loss can be of equipment, data, or software/licences
Unauthorised software causes licence/legal liability and compatibility issues
Unauthorised software may be used for spying, harassment or to avoid monitoring

items.definition: Physical events that damage IT systems and the data they hold. These can be natural, accidental or deliberate.
items.examples: A burst pipe flooding a server room; an arson attack; a power cut corrupting unsaved data.
items.examTip: These threats justify off-site/cloud backups and disaster recovery plans (link to A4 and C1).
keyFacts: Includes fire, flood, power loss, terrorism and other disasters
Causes loss of both hardware and the data stored on it
Mitigated by off-site backups, UPS, fire suppression and DR plans

items.definition: Poor habits and weak controls that make an organisation easier to attack, such as not securing equipment, not vetting visitors, or browsing untrustworthy websites.
items.examples: Leaving a server room unlocked; letting a visitor wander unescorted; staff visiting dodgy download sites on work PCs.
items.examTip: Unsafe practices are a 'human' vulnerability — the fix is usually training and policy, not just technology.
keyFacts: Poor physical security of equipment and storage devices
No security vetting of visitors
Visiting untrustworthy websites that host malware

items.term: Accidental Loss/Disclosure of Data or Credentials
items.definition: Sensitive data or login details being exposed through human factors rather than a deliberate attack.
items.examples: Emailing a spreadsheet of customer details to the wrong address; writing a password on a sticky note; losing an unencrypted laptop.
items.examTip: Root causes are negligence, poor training and not following procedures — caused by a weak security culture.
keyFacts: Human factors: negligence, poor training, not following procedures
Made worse by inadequate monitoring and reporting
Underlying cause is often a weak security culture

items.definition: Malicious code that attaches to a host file or program and replicates when that file is run, spreading to other files and systems.
items.examples: A macro virus hidden in a Word document; a boot sector virus that loads before the OS.
items.examTip: Know the named types: boot sector, web script, macro, worm, rootkit, trojan, browser hijack, polymorphic.
keyFacts: Boot sector — infects the start-up area of a disk
Macro — hidden in document macros (e.g. Office files)
Worm — self-replicates across networks without a host file
Rootkit — hides deep in the OS to avoid detection
Trojan — disguised as legitimate software
Polymorphic — changes its code to evade signature scanning

items.definition: Software that secretly gathers information about a user and sends it to a third party without consent.
items.examples: A keylogger recording passwords as they are typed; stalkerware tracking a phone's location; tracking cookies following browsing habits.
items.examTip: Keylogger = records keystrokes to steal credentials. This is a favourite exam term.
keyFacts: Keylogger/data thief — records keystrokes to steal credentials
System monitor — captures all activity on a device
Mobile tracker/stalkerware — secretly tracks location/usage
Web beacons and tracking cookies — monitor online behaviour

items.definition: Software that automatically displays or downloads advertising. Ranges from legitimate ad-supported software to abusive/deceptive adware.
items.examples: A free app showing pop-up ads; a 'potentially unwanted program' (PUP) bundled with a download.
items.examTip: Not all adware is illegal — distinguish legitimate adware from abusive/deceptive (and sometimes illegal) adware.
keyFacts: Potentially Unwanted Program (PUP) — installed alongside other software
Legitimate adware funds free software with consent
Abusive/deceptive adware tricks users and can be illegal

items.definition: Malware that blocks access to data or systems — usually by encrypting files — and demands payment (a ransom) to restore access.
items.examples: An 'encryptor' scrambling all company files; a 'locker' freezing the whole screen; 'leakware' threatening to publish stolen data.
items.examTip: Best defence is reliable, tested OFFLINE backups so you can restore without paying. Link to A4.1.2 / C1.1.3.
keyFacts: Encryptors — encrypt files so they cannot be opened
Lockers — lock the device/screen entirely
Scareware — fake warnings pressuring the user to pay
Leakware/doxware — threatens to publish stolen data
Defence: tested offline backups, patching, staff awareness

items.definition: Compromised computers controlled remotely by an attacker. A network of bots (a botnet) can be used to launch large-scale attacks such as DDoS.
items.examples: Thousands of infected IoT devices used together to flood a website with traffic.
items.examTip: Bots/botnets connect malware (A1.2.1) to DDoS attacks (A1.2.2) — a common exam link.
keyFacts: An infected device under remote attacker control
Many bots together form a botnet
Used to send spam or launch DDoS attacks

items.definition: Gaining unauthorised access to systems or data, targeting commercial organisations, governments or individuals.
items.examples: A DDoS attack taking a website offline; defacing a public web page (front-end tampering); altering records in a database (back-end tampering).
items.examTip: DoS = one source; DDoS = many sources (a botnet). Distinguish front-end vs back-end data tampering.
keyFacts: DoS — one machine floods a target to make it unavailable
DDoS — many machines (botnet) flood the target
Data theft — stealing confidential information
Data tampering — altering back-end databases or front-end web pages
Cyberwarfare — state-sponsored attacks on infrastructure

items.definition: Deliberately damaging, destroying or corrupting data, systems or infrastructure — by commercial rivals, governments, individuals or terrorists.
items.examples: Poisoning the data used to train an AI; creating AI-generated deepfake video; hijacking internet-connected industrial machinery.
items.examTip: 'Fakes' now explicitly includes AI-generated images/video/audio — a modern exam topic.
keyFacts: Data poisoning, tampering and destruction
Fakes — images/video/audio/documents made manually or with AI
Damage to/hijacking of machinery, vehicles, IoT devices
Targets can include critical national infrastructure

items.definition: Manipulating or deceiving people into giving away secure information, rather than attacking technology directly.
items.examples: A phishing email pretending to be from the bank; a vishing phone call impersonating IT support; spear phishing aimed at one named employee.
items.examTip: Know the variants: phishing (email), vishing (voice), smishing (SMS), whaling (senior targets), spear phishing (specific target).
keyFacts: Phishing (email), vishing (phone), smishing (SMS)
Whaling — targets senior executives; spear phishing — targets a specific person
DNS spoofing — redirects users to fake sites
Pretexting/impersonation — inventing a scenario to gain trust
Best defence is staff training and awareness

items.definition: Threats that rely on physically reaching a secure area or device rather than attacking over a network.
items.examples: Tailgating through a controlled door behind a staff member; shoulder surfing a password; stealing an unattended laptop.
items.examTip: Tailgating (following someone through a secure door) appeared in the sample paper — learn the one-line definition.
keyFacts: Unauthorised area access: tailgating, forced entry, impersonation, coercion
Unauthorised device access: unattended devices, shoulder surfing, theft, lost devices
Devices in public areas are especially exposed

items.definition: The impact on an organisation's ability to function and deliver its products or services.
items.examples: A factory production line halting after a ransomware attack; a website being unavailable so customers cannot order.
items.examTip: Operational = the business can't operate. Cover output, service availability and data availability.
keyFacts: Loss of manufacturing output
Loss of service availability
Loss of data availability

items.definition: The monetary cost of an incident to the organisation, including lost income, compensation and legal liability.
items.examples: GDPR fines after a breach; refunds and identity-protection costs for affected customers; legal fees.
items.examTip: Break financial loss into organisational costs, compensation and legal liability for full marks.
keyFacts: Organisational: cash flow problems, loss of profits, higher insurance
Compensation: refunds, payments for compromised data, remedial costs
Legal liability: fines, penalty payments, legal fees

items.definition: Damage to how customers and the public view an organisation following an incident.
items.examples: Customers leaving negative reviews on social media; a drop in trust scores after a publicised breach.
items.examTip: Reputational damage is often the longest-lasting impact — lost trust is hard to rebuild. Great point for 9-markers.
keyFacts: Loss of customer trust
Poor reviews on social media, review sites and own website
Reduced scores on reputation metrics

items.definition: The theft or exposure of an organisation's valuable confidential ideas and information.
items.examples: A competitor stealing a new product design or trade secret; leaked testing and development data.
items.examTip: IP loss can destroy competitive advantage even if no personal data is involved.
keyFacts: New product designs
Testing and development data
Organisational strategy and trade secrets

items.definition: The National Cyber Security Centre — the UK's authority on cyber security, providing threat reports, malware analysis, advisories and guidance.
items.examples: Checking the NCSC website for the latest ransomware advisory.
items.examTip: NCSC = UK. Provides up-to-date threat reports because threats change over time.
keyFacts: UK government body for cyber security
Publishes latest threat reports and malware analysis
Issues news, advisories and guidance on recent activity

items.definition: The National Institute of Standards and Technology — a US body that issues cyber security news, standards and advisories.
items.examples: Referencing NIST guidance on password policy.
items.examTip: NIST = USA equivalent of NCSC. Sets widely-used security standards.
keyFacts: US standards organisation
Publishes news and advisories on recent activity
Produces widely-adopted security frameworks

items.definition: The Open Web Application Security Project — a non-profit producing the OWASP Top 10, a regularly updated list of the most critical web application security risks.
items.examples: Using the OWASP Top 10 to check a website for SQL injection risks.
items.examTip: OWASP Top 10 is referenced in penetration testing (A2.6). Link the two.
keyFacts: Focuses on web application security
Publishes the OWASP Top 10 critical risks
Used as a checklist during penetration testing

items.definition: Weaknesses in network configuration that attackers can exploit, especially around firewall ports and external storage devices.
items.examples: An open port 80 left exposed; a USB flash drive carrying malware onto the network.
items.examTip: Know the three port categories: well-known (e.g. 80 for HTTP), registered, and dynamic/private. Open ports = a vulnerability.
keyFacts: Firewall ports: well-known (e.g. 80/HTTP), registered, dynamic/private
Port vulnerabilities: open ports, spoofing, DoS
External storage (USB, SD, external HDD, SSD, optical/tape) can introduce malware

items.definition: Weaknesses in how an organisation manages permissions, passwords and accounts.
items.examples: Giving every user administrator rights; allowing weak, reused passwords; not disabling a leaver's account.
items.examTip: Password policy elements (min/max length, character rules, reuse frequency, minimum age) are common 'state two' marks.
keyFacts: Permissions: read/write/execute/modify for user/admin/system/group
Password policy: length, character rules, reuse frequency, minimum age
Password management: password managers, lockout of inactive accounts, leaver process
Auto-fill by browser or dedicated software can be a risk

items.definition: Weaknesses introduced by untrustworthy, outdated or poorly designed software.
items.examples: Installing pirated software with a backdoor; an unpatched web app vulnerable to SQL injection; a zero-day exploit.
items.examTip: Zero-day = a brand new flaw with no patch yet, leaving a window of exploitation. SQL injection appears in the sample paper.
keyFacts: Untrustworthy sources / malicious installers
Safe downloads need: trusted source, HTTPS, pre-install malware scan, hash check
Illegal copies lack updates and may contain backdoors/malware
Zero-day exploits — new threats before a patch exists
SQL injection and missing patches/updates

items.definition: Weaknesses in the operating system and its interfaces, usually from being out of date or misconfigured.
items.examples: Running an unsupported version of Windows; missing security patches; insecure default settings.
items.examTip: Unsupported/out-of-support software is a key vulnerability because it no longer receives security patches.
keyFacts: Unsupported/out-of-support versions
Missing patches/updates
Missing or incorrect security settings

items.definition: Mobile devices rely on Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEMs) to release system software updates, so they can be left unpatched.
items.examples: An old Android phone no longer receiving security updates from its manufacturer.
items.examTip: The key point: reliance on OEMs means updates may be slow or stop, leaving known flaws unpatched.
keyFacts: Updates depend on the device manufacturer (OEM)
Older devices may stop receiving updates
Leaves known vulnerabilities unpatched

items.definition: Weaknesses that allow theft of, or physical access to, equipment holding sensitive data.
items.examples: Stealing a mobile device or data storage device; weak security on a restricted area.
items.examTip: Physical vulnerabilities are mitigated by physical security measures (A4.1.1) — link them.
keyFacts: Theft of equipment/devices holding sensitive data
Vulnerable mobile devices and data storage devices
Poor or missing security for restricted areas

items.definition: Weaknesses arising from how people actually use the system day to day.
items.examples: An employee sharing their login; a flawed process that lets data leave the organisation unchecked.
items.examTip: These are 'human' vulnerabilities — fixed by training, policy and good processes.
keyFacts: Leaks, both intentional and accidental
Sharing security details
Flawed security processes

items.definition: Security risks specific to cloud computing and Internet of Things devices.
items.examples: A misconfigured cloud bucket exposing data; an IoT camera with a default password being hijacked.
items.examTip: IoT risks (default passwords, no encryption, no patches, always-listening) are a modern hot topic — learn several.
keyFacts: Cloud: default/incorrect settings, third-party access, reliance on provider, data leaving the network
IoT: weak/no encryption, default passwords, lack of patches
IoT: deployment by non-IT staff, insecure interfaces, eavesdropping (always listening)

items.definition: Where to find up-to-date information about known hardware and software vulnerabilities.
items.examples: Checking a manufacturer's website for a firmware fix; reading a security forum for IT professionals.
items.examTip: Three named sources: manufacturer's website, professional forums/help sites, specialist third-party sites.
keyFacts: Manufacturer's website
Forums/technical help sites for IT and security professionals
Third-party sites specialising in specific hardware/software

items.definition: The routes or pathways an attacker uses to reach a system — wireless links, internet connections and internal network devices.
items.examples: Attacking over Wi-Fi or Bluetooth; intercepting a connection at the router; exploiting a switch or access point.
items.examTip: An attack vector is the 'way in'. Wireless vectors include Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, satellite, IR, NFC and RFID.
keyFacts: Wireless: Wi-Fi (802.11), Bluetooth, cellular, satellite, IR, NFC, RFID
Internet connection: copper, optical fibre, Wi-Fi, cellular/5G + their devices
Internal access devices: router, switch, wireless access point

items.definition: Software tools used to find weaknesses in computer systems before attackers do.
items.examples: A port scanner checking which ports are open; a website vulnerability scanner testing a web app.
items.examTip: Know the named tools: port scanner, network mapper, registry checker, website vulnerability scanner.
keyFacts: Port scanner and network mapper/system discovery
Registry checker and website vulnerability scanner
Vulnerability detection/management software
Assessing user vulnerabilities (e.g. phishing simulations)

items.definition: Having an external expert review system and network designs before they are implemented.
items.examples: Hiring a consultancy to review a new network design and certify it.
items.examTip: Purpose: establishes due diligence and provides independent third-party certification.
keyFacts: Done before implementation
Establishes due diligence
Provides third-party certification

items.definition: Authorised simulated attacks on a system to find weak spots, checking against known vulnerabilities such as the OWASP Top 10.
items.examples: A 'pen tester' attempting to break into a network and producing a report of weaknesses found.
items.examTip: Pen testing uses real attack techniques but with permission, then produces a report. Links to OWASP (A1.4.3).
keyFacts: Uses a range of techniques to find weak spots
Checks against lists of known vulnerabilities (OWASP Top 10)
Produces reports in appropriate formats

items.definition: Ways of managing risk that do not involve adding active security controls: transferring, avoiding or accepting the risk.
items.examples: Buying cyber insurance (transfer); stopping a risky activity (avoidance); accepting a small, low-impact risk.
items.examTip: Three passive options: transfer (e.g. insurance/3rd party), avoid (stop the activity), accept (live with it).
keyFacts: Risk transfer — pass it to a third party (e.g. insurer/provider)
Risk avoidance — stop the risky activity
Risk acceptance — acknowledge and tolerate the risk

items.definition: Legislation setting out requirements for protecting personal data and the privacy rights of individuals.
items.examples: An organisation must get consent before collecting data and must report a breach within 72 hours.
items.examTip: GDPR = personal data + privacy rights. Computer Misuse Act = unauthorised access. Don't mix them up.
keyFacts: Protects personal data and privacy rights
Applies to data in storage and when transferred
Covers personally identifying information (PII)

items.definition: Legislation that protects personal data held by organisations from unauthorised access and modification.
items.examples: Hacking into a system you have no permission to access is an offence under this Act.
items.examTip: Computer Misuse Act = unauthorised access to/modification of computers and data.
keyFacts: Covers unauthorised access to computers/devices
Covers unauthorised access to and modification of data
Makes hacking and creating malware criminal offences

items.definition: The core rules organisations must follow when processing personal data.
items.examples: Only collecting the minimum data needed, keeping it accurate, and deleting it when no longer required.
items.examTip: Remember key principles: lawful/fair/transparent, purpose limited, accurate, minimal, kept minimum time, confidential.
keyFacts: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency
Limited to a stated purpose; accuracy
Keep the minimum amount of data for the minimum time
Maintain confidentiality and integrity

items.definition: An organisation must have a valid legal basis to process personal data.
items.examples: Processing payroll data under 'contractual obligation'; using medical data under 'vital interest'.
items.examTip: Six lawful bases: consent, contract, legitimate interest, vital interest, legal requirement, public interest.
keyFacts: Consent and contractual obligation
Legitimate interest and vital interest
Legal requirement and public interest

items.definition: The rights individuals have over their own personal data under GDPR.
items.examples: A customer requesting a copy of all data held on them (access), or asking for it to be deleted.
items.examTip: Key rights: access, be informed, correct/remove/restrict, object, portability, no solely-automated decisions.
keyFacts: Right to access their own data and be informed how it is used
Right to have data corrected, removed or restricted
Right to object, and to data portability (machine-readable format)
Right not to be subject to a solely automated decision

items.definition: Measures that physically protect equipment, sites and restricted areas from unauthorised access.
items.examples: RFID card entry; fingerprint scanners; CCTV; security staff; alarms; locked server cabinets.
items.examTip: Group these into: locks, card entry, biometrics, surveillance (CCTV/staff/alarms), and staff training.
keyFacts: Site locks: mechanical, electronic, network-connected
Card entry: NFC, RFID, barcode/QR, magnetic stripe, chip
Biometrics: fingerprint, iris/retina, facial, voice, signature
CCTV, security staff, alarms, protected cabling, staff training

items.definition: Strategies for copying data so it can be restored after loss, corruption or attack.
items.examples: A full weekly backup plus daily incremental backups stored off-site and in the cloud.
items.examTip: Know the 3 backup types: FULL (everything), INCREMENTAL (changes since last backup), DIFFERENTIAL (changes since last full). RAID is NOT a backup.
keyFacts: Types: full, differential, incremental
Strategies: onsite/offsite/cloud, automated/manual, hot/warm site
RAID and archiving are NOT the same as backup
Recovery: file restore, image restore, full/bare-metal restore

items.definition: Software that detects, blocks and removes malware using signatures, heuristics and integrity checks.
items.examples: Quarantining a suspicious file; matching a file against known virus signatures.
items.examTip: Signature scanning catches known malware; heuristics catch new/suspicious behaviour. Know both.
keyFacts: Virus signatures and scanning (known threats)
Heuristics — flag suspicious behaviour/new threats
File integrity check / checksum
Responses: warning, logging, prevent execution, quarantine, deletion

items.definition: Hardware or software that filters network traffic using rules to block unauthorised access.
items.examples: A firewall blocking inbound traffic on all ports except those needed; application-layer filtering.
items.examTip: Firewalls use inbound and outbound rules and can do packet filtering and application-layer awareness.
keyFacts: Packet filtering and inspection
Application-layer awareness
Inbound and outbound rules
Filtering by network address

items.definition: Verifying that a user is who they claim to be, often using multiple factors (MFA).
items.examples: Password + USB security key; fingerprint + PIN; an authenticator app code.
items.examTip: MFA factors: knowledge (something you know), possession (have), inherence (are), plus location/behaviour. USB security key = possession factor (sample paper).
keyFacts: Single-factor vs multi-factor authentication (MFA)
Factors: knowledge, possession, inherence, location, behaviour
Security tokens: connected (USB key), contactless, disconnected (code generator)
Kerberos, key exchange, and certificate-based authentication (TLS/SSL, PKI, CA)

items.definition: Methods that restrict which users can access which resources.
items.examples: Role-Based Access Control giving the finance team access to accounts but not HR files.
items.examTip: DAC = users control their own files; Role-Based = by job role; Rule-Based = rules per individual user.
keyFacts: Discretionary Access Control (DAC) — users control their own resources
Role-Based Access Control — access set by role in the organisation
Rule-Based Access Control — rules set for individual users
Applies to apps, folders, files, datasets, physical devices

items.definition: Hardware-based security (e.g. a trusted platform) that increases security but can reduce user control.
items.examples: A TPM chip checking the system is in a trusted state before allowing access.
items.examTip: Trusted computing appeared in the sample paper — benefit: increased security; drawback: loss of user control/privacy.
keyFacts: Benefit: increased security / another layer of protection
Drawback: loss of user control, privacy and anonymity

items.definition: Measures that protect devices and allow lost or stolen ones to be located, locked or wiped.
items.examples: Using GPS 'find my device'; remotely wiping a stolen phone; auto-locking the screen after failed logins.
items.examTip: Remote lock/wipe and timed lockout are strong answers for protecting a lost/stolen device.
keyFacts: Location tech: GPS, phone-home, tracking software
Timed lockout of screen; lock after failed login attempts
Memory wipe/factory reset after failed attempts
Remote lock/wipe/reset of lost or stolen devices

items.definition: Encrypting data at rest so it is unreadable if the device or media is stolen.
items.examples: Full-disk encryption on a laptop; encrypting an individual confidential file or folder.
items.examTip: Storage encryption protects data 'at rest' — vital for lost/stolen devices. Link to A4.1.9.
keyFacts: Safe password storage
Digital Rights Management (DRM)
File, folder, disc and device encryption

items.definition: Encrypting data in transit so it cannot be read if intercepted.
items.examples: HTTPS securing a website; a VPN encrypting remote-worker traffic; end-to-end encrypted messaging.
items.examTip: Symmetric = one shared secret key (AES, fast); asymmetric = public+private key pair (RSA). Know the difference.
keyFacts: Symmetric: one secret key, e.g. AES (fast)
Asymmetric: public + private keys, e.g. RSA, Diffie-Hellman
Used in TOR, VPNs, HTTPS, digital certificates
End-to-End Encryption (E2EE) in secure messaging apps

items.definition: Precautions that protect a wireless LAN from unauthorised access.
items.examples: Using WPA3 encryption; hiding the SSID; MAC address filtering; changing default passwords.
items.examTip: MAC filtering and WPA2/WPA3 appear in the sample paper. Remember MAC addresses can be spoofed (so 'medium' security).
keyFacts: MAC address filtering and hiding the SSID
Wireless encryption: WPA2/WPA3, Wi-Fi Protected Setup
Known attacks: unsecured AP, piggybacking, Evil Twin, sniffing
Mitigation: change defaults, allow/block lists, VPNs, WPA2/3, firewalls

items.definition: Principles that build security into a system from the start, rather than adding it later.
items.examples: Designing with 'least privilege' and assuming attackers will try to get in.
items.examTip: Key principles: expect attacks, least privilege, don't rely on secrecy, comply with standards (ISO 27000).
keyFacts: Expect attacks and plan for them
Run on fewest privileges (least privilege)
Assume the design will be known — avoid relying on secrecy/obscurity
Comply with standards such as ISO 27000
